sections.h2: Where is the Lincoln County Recorder of Deeds office?
sections.html:
The Lincoln County Recorder of Deeds works from the county courthouse at 201 Main Street in Troy, Missouri 63379. Troy is the county seat, and the recorder's page on the county site lists Tracy Martin as Recorder of Deeds with a chief deputy clerk and two deputy clerks. For questions about fees, the county's own alert notice gives 636-528-0325.

Any real estate document handed in after 3:30 pm is recorded the next business day. If your closing is set for late in the afternoon, ask your title company when the deed will be delivered to Troy so the recording date matches what you expect.

The office checks that a document meets the statutory requirements for recording. Staff cannot give legal advice, run title or lien searches, fill in or type deeds, supply blank forms, decide who owns a property, or act as a notary. That work belongs to an attorney or a title company.

sections.h2: What does the Lincoln County recorder actually record?
sections.html:
The recorder keeps the county's real estate records and marriage license records. Deeds, deeds of trust, releases, easements, surveys, plats, restrictions, wills, road rights of way, affidavits and patents all go on file there, along with servicemen's records and tax liens on request.

Missouri law gives the recording step real weight. Under RSMo 442.380, a written instrument that conveys land must be recorded in the county where the land sits. Under RSMo 442.400, an unrecorded instrument is valid only between the parties and anyone with actual notice of it. A buyer who skips recording leaves the sale open to later claims, so the deed goes to Troy the same week it is signed.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to record a deed in Lincoln County?
sections.html:
The county's posted fee schedule puts a standard real estate document at $26.00 for the first page and $3.00 for each added page. A county notice tied to Senate Bill 938 announced a $2.00 increase effective August 28, 2026, and it states the first-page fee at $26.00 after that increase. That date has passed, so $26.00 is the figure to plan around.

State law sets a lower base. RSMo 59.310 lists $5 for the first page and $3 for each page after it. The county schedule is the number that matters at the counter, and your title company will carry it on the settlement statement.

sections.h2: What format rules can get a Lincoln County deed rejected?
sections.html:
The recorder will turn away a document that misses the formatting rules, and a rejected deed delays your closing funds. The county page and RSMo 59.310 point to the same checklist:

  • A blank top margin of 3 inches on the first page, kept clear for the recorder's certification.
  • Margins of three-quarters of an inch on the other three sides.
  • A legible legal description of the property.
  • A proper notarization, with the notary's signature legible and the seal legibly placed beneath it.
  • No handwritten documents.
  • Type no smaller than eight-point, in black or dark ink, on white or light paper.

Section 59.310 also allows a recorder to take a document that fails the format test for an added $25 fee, and it lists exempt categories such as documents signed before January 1, 2002 and documents executed outside the United States. The first page must show the title, date, grantors with marital status, grantees, any statutory addresses and the legal description. Have your closing agent prepare the deed to these specifications.

sections.h2: What happens to property tax when a Lincoln County house sells?
sections.html:
Once a deed is recorded, the recorder passes the transfer to the County Assessor, who updates ownership and the mailing address on the tax file. The Lincoln County Collector's guidance says taxes are normally prorated between buyer and seller at closing, with the seller's share credited to the buyer on the settlement statement. The buyer then pays the full bill when it arrives at the end of the year.

  • The assessor closes the files around August 31 so the collector can print the tax books, and a name cannot be changed once the books are printed.
  • If a bill arrives in your name after you sold, check the settlement sheet and ask the collector to confirm payment. The receipt covers the full year, and your settlement sheet is your proof of the share you paid.
  • A wrong name or legal description on the assessor's records is fixed by recording a corrected deed.
  • After November 1, the closing agent usually pays the tax at closing, but any unpaid amount stays with the new owner.

The collector also notes that Missouri requires a parcel with three years of unpaid tax to be offered at public auction, and that lender foreclosure sales follow different rules with no required courthouse posting.

sections.h2: What does Lincoln County look like for a home seller?
sections.html:
Lincoln County sits in eastern Missouri along the Mississippi River, which forms its border with Illinois, and it belongs to the St. Louis metropolitan area. The county covers about 627 square miles of land. U.S. Route 61 and Missouri routes 47, 79 and 147 cross it, and BNSF Railway runs through. Communities named in county records include Troy, Winfield, Moscow Mills, Old Monroe, Elsberry, Silex and Hawk Point.

The Census Bureau shows a county that has grown fast. The population estimate for July 2025 is 66,676, up 11.9 percent from the 2020 base, against 52,566 in 2010. Housing units number 24,289, and the owner-occupied rate is 79.0 percent. Median value of an owner-occupied home for 2020 to 2024 is $244,300, and median household income is $89,278. Workers face a mean commute of 31.8 minutes, and the county issued 252 building permits in 2025.

Public schools come from several districts: Troy R-III, Winfield R-IV, Elsberry R-II and Silex R-I, with Wright City R-II covering southern portions.

sections.h2: How do you move a Lincoln County deed from signing to the public record?
sections.html:
1. Have the deed drafted by an attorney or title company, since the recorder cannot type or fill in deeds.
  2. Sign before a notary, and confirm the seal and signature are legible.
  3. Check the first page for the 3 inch top margin and the legal description.
  4. Pay the county fee, which is $26.00 for page one of a standard document plus $3.00 for each added page.
  5. Deliver the deed to Troy before 3:30 pm if you want same-day recording.
  6. Ask the Assessor's office to confirm the ownership change on its file.

Title companies handle these steps as routine work on a Lincoln County closing. If you are selling an inherited house, a small estate affidavit and certificate can also be recorded with the recorder to show heirs' title, so bring the probate paperwork to your closing agent early.

faqs.q: Does the Lincoln County recorder charge a transfer tax?
faqs.a: The county's fee schedule lists recording charges only, with no transfer tax line. Ask your title company to itemize every charge on the settlement statement, and call the recorder at 636-528-0325 if a line looks unfamiliar.

faqs.q: How much is the first page fee for a deed in Lincoln County?
faqs.a: A standard real estate document costs $26.00 for the first page and $3.00 for each added page. A document the county classes as non-standard costs $49.00 for the first page.

faqs.q: Can the recorder help me write my deed?
faqs.a: No. The office checks that a document meets recording requirements but does not draft or type deeds, supply forms, give legal advice or run title searches. Use an attorney or a title company.

faqs.q: What time must I deliver a document to get it recorded the same day?
faqs.a: Before 3:30 pm. Documents presented after that time are recorded the next business day.

faqs.q: Do I have to record a deed after selling my Lincoln County house?
faqs.a: Yes. Missouri law requires a conveyance of land to be recorded in the county where the land lies, and an unrecorded deed is valid only between the parties and anyone with actual notice. Your closing agent normally files it for you.
